summary: This proposed standard defines MIB objects for managing DS3 and E3 interfaces, which are faster telephone-company style digital links. It was replaced by RFC 2496.

eli5.summary: This is a checklist of things a network manager can ask about a big, fast digital phone-line connection, like whether it is working properly.

questions: what is the ds3 e3 mib
what is the difference between ds3 and e3 snmp objects
how long are ds3 performance intervals
subtitle: SNMP objects for configuring and monitoring DS3 and E3 high-speed digital line interfaces.

tldr.problem: Devices with DS3 and E3 lines had no common SNMP view of their configuration, error counts and alarms, and the earlier attempt in RFC 1233 encoded many objects with the wrong type.
tldr.mechanism: The MIB defines a mandatory near end group, an optional far end group and an optional fractional group, with 15-minute performance intervals, error and defect terminology, and an index scheme tying lines to MIB-II interfaces.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1407 fully replaces RFC 1233, which should not be implemented, and was itself obsoleted by RFC 2496.

today: RFC 1407 is a Proposed Standard that was obsoleted by RFC 2496, so use that document for the current DS3/E3 MIB. It replaced RFC 1233, which should not be implemented.

sections.title: Scope and Why It Replaced RFC 1233
sections.content:
RFC 1407 defines an extension to the Management Information Base (MIB) for managing DS3 and E3 interfaces. It is a companion to the definitions for the DS1 interface type. It applies when the interface is of ifType ds3 (30) in the Internet-standard MIB, and the objects live under transmission 30.

The memo entirely replaces RFC 1233, which had a fundamental error: many objects were encoded as Counters that must be INTEGERs or Gauges. The change was so large that virtually every object changed, so the MIB in RFC 1233 should not be implemented. DS3 definitions are based on ANSI specifications and the E3 definitions on CCITT G.751.
sections.eli5: The first version used the wrong kind of counter for almost everything, so this memo is the fixed copy and the old one should be thrown away.

sections.title: What Changed from RFC 1233
sections.content:
Besides changing every Counter to a Gauge, the memo adds the following:

  • E3 interfaces are now covered too.
  • There are three groups: the DS3/E3 Near End Group (mandatory), the DS3 Far End Group (optional) and the DS3 Fractional Group (optional).
  • The Far End Group holds configuration and statistics collected from the far end interface, and may only be implemented by DS3 systems that use C-bit Parity or SYNTRAN.
  • New objects: dsx3LoopbackConfig, dsx3LineStatus and dsx3TransmitClockSource. dsx3SendCode now reflects different loopback messages.
  • Line Coding Violations are counted instead of Bipolar Violations, and a Line Errored Seconds object is added to all near end tables.
  • P-bit and C-bit counts are kept apart: the original coding violation and errored second counters were renamed to PCV, PES and PSES, and new C-bit counters were added.
sections.eli5: The new version adds a second set of questions about the other end of the cable, and it keeps two kinds of error checks separate.

sections.title: Indexes and Error Terminology
sections.content:
Two indexes tie lines to the Interfaces table of MIB-II. dsx3IfIndex always equals ifIndex. dsx3LineIndex identifies a DS3/E3 line on a device. When the SNMP agent sits on the device that has the lines, ifIndex, dsx3IfIndex and dsx3LineIndex are all equal. In a router-plus-CSU setup, the router-side and network-side lines each get their own dsx3LineIndex, numbered above ifNumber, with even numbers for equipment-side lines and odd numbers for network-side ones.

The design aligns closely with the objects that can generally be read from deployed DS3/E3 devices. It defines error events such as Bipolar Violations, Excessive Zeros, Line Coding Violations, P-bit Coding Violations and C-bit Coding Violations. Performance parameters such as Line Errored Seconds and Unavailable Seconds are built from those, and defects such as Loss of Signal, Out of Frame and Alarm Indication Signal can lead to failure states.
sections.eli5: Each cable end gets its own number, and the memo explains what counts as a bad second, so every maker counts mistakes the same way.

sections.title: The Three Groups and Their Tables
sections.content:
The near end group is mandatory for all systems that attach to a DS3/E3 interface and has four tables: Configuration, Current, Interval and Total. The Configuration table includes dsx3LineType (such as M23, SYNTRAN, C-bit Parity or the E3 framings), dsx3LineCoding (B3ZS or HDB3), dsx3LoopbackConfig (no loop, payload loop, line loop or other loop), dsx3CircuitIdentifier and dsx3LineStatus.

The optional far end group has its own configuration, current, interval and total tables. The optional fractional group is modeled after the DS1 Fractional Group.

All performance parameters are accumulated in fifteen-minute intervals, and an agent keeps up to 96 intervals, which is 24 hours. There is also a rolling 24-hour total. Fewer than 96 intervals will be available if the agent restarted in the last 24 hours.
sections.eli5: The equipment keeps a notebook with a page for now, a page for each quarter hour of the last day, and a page with the day's total.

sections.title: Security
sections.content: The Security Considerations section says only that security issues are not discussed in this memo. The memo relies on the Internet-standard Network Management Framework: the SMI in RFC 1155 and RFC 1212, MIB-II in RFC 1213, and SNMP in RFC 1157.
sections.eli5: The memo does not say anything about keeping the information private.
